Four Turtles

GeometryCurvesInvariants
Game: Watch four turtles chase each other around a square and see how far each one crawls before they meet.
How to play: Press Let them go to start and Stop to pause. Choose a frame, a number of turtles and whether to trace their paths; drag the outside dial, focus it and use the arrow keys, or type a number to change the count.
Look for the math

Four turtles start at the corners of a square, each crawling toward the next at the same steady speed. They spiral into the middle together. The surprising part is that the distance each turtle travels depends only on the starting side and the number of turtles — and for four turtles it is exactly one side.

The shape never changes

Because every turtle does the same thing, the picture has symmetry: after any amount of time the turtles still sit at the corners of a smaller regular polygon with the same centre. It has only turned and shrunk. The applet applies the same turn-and-shrink map to all the corners; the logic test checked every side of 2,486 painted frames, for every turtle count from 3 to 20, and found the sides equal and evenly spaced each time.

Time and distance, no calculus needed

Let the side be S, the distance from the centre to a corner R, and a = pi/N. A corner of a regular polygon gives S/2 = R sin(a). A turtle's speed points along a side, so only V sin(a) of it points towards the centre. The turtle has R to go:

T = R / (V sin(a)) = S / (2 V sin²(a)) = S / (V (1 − cos(2a)))
D = V T = S / (1 − cos(2a))

For N = 4, cos(2a) = cos(pi/2) = 0, so D = S: a turtle walks exactly one side of the square, and the time is S/V. A triangle gives D = 2S/3; with five turtles D is about 1.45 S. The test checked all three forms of T and the identity D = VT for 504 combinations of N, side and speed, and found no disagreement. This is the page's central claim, and it holds exactly (up to rounding).

Two frames, one chase

Ride along with the turning polygon and the turtles seem to come straight towards the centre, while the first polygon appears to turn the other way. That is just a change of viewpoint: the applet negates its turn in the rotating frame and keeps the shrinking polygon on fixed rays from the centre. In a still frame the paths are logarithmic spirals, r = c ekt in polar coordinates: each small step towards the middle turns more than the last. The test confirmed both: every trace point satisfies ratio = exp(angle/k), and the turn grows on every later frame.

One honest difference: the physical pursuit angle is −cot(a) log(r/R), which the page derives, but the old applet turns by sin(g)(1 − cos(g)) log(s/S) with g = pi(N−2)/N. Those coefficients agree only for N = 4; for other counts the animation is a log spiral of a different pitch. The page's formula is the right one for equal-speed pursuit; the applet's constant is a display choice that keeps the picture watchable. This page keeps the applet's animation numbers.

What the old controls did

The applet started with N = 4 and allowed 3 to 20, with radius trunc((min(width, height) − 40)/2) and side 2R sin(pi/N). Every 50 ms it reduced the side by speed(N)(1 − cos(g)) and repainted. For four turtles that step is 12 in the applet's units, so the side falls linearly as S = S0 − Vt, as the page says. Trace unlocked Spirals, Whirl and Both; Whirl started selected, Trace started off. The test transcribed Reset(), Transform.Apply() and run() a second time and compared all 216 configurations, frame by frame and point by point. The applet's own about-box still says "Shapes of Constant Width", a harmless leftover copied from a sibling; it has nothing to do with turtles.

Try Rotating with Trace and Both turned on: the straight radial approach and the turning original square make the change of viewpoint easy to see.
